drills.q: Why is a tree walking interpreter slow?
options: It pays a dispatch and a pointer chase for every node, including the leaves
It reparses the source at every step
It cannot use the processor's arithmetic instructions
It allocates a new stack frame per operation
drills.why: The arithmetic is the cheap part. The nodes were allocated separately and sit in different cache lines, which is why the measured gap to a bytecode machine is a factor of ten and not a factor of two.

drills.q: What does compiling to bytecode buy over walking the tree?
options: The tree is walked once, and what runs afterwards is a dense array with good locality
The program is compiled to machine code before it runs
Types are checked ahead of time rather than at each operation
Dispatch is eliminated entirely
drills.why: Dispatch is still paid per instruction. What goes away is the per-node pointer chase, and the compile step can fold constants and cache the result.

drills.q: What is the difference between a stack machine and a register machine?
options: One takes operands from an operand stack; the other names them as slots in the frame
One runs on the hardware stack; the other uses hardware registers
One is interpreted and the other is compiled
One is for dynamic languages and the other for static ones
drills.why: It is about where an instruction says its operands are. Naming them makes instructions fatter and fewer.

drills.q: Which executes more instructions for the same work?
options: The stack machine, because pushing and popping are instructions too
The register machine, because its instructions are larger
They execute the same number by definition
It depends only on the language being interpreted
drills.why: Adding two locals is four instructions on a stack machine and one on a register machine. Dispatch is where the time goes, so that matters.

drills.q: Why does a switch based dispatch loop hurt branch prediction?
options: Every opcode shares one indirect branch site, so the predictor cannot learn which opcode follows which
The jump table is too large for the cache
A switch compiles to a chain of comparisons
Indirect branches are never predicted at all
drills.why: From that one site the target is whatever the program happens to be doing next, so there is no correlation to learn.

drills.q: What does ending each opcode body with its own jump achieve?
options: One branch site per opcode, so the predictor can learn sequences like compare then jump
Fewer instructions executed per opcode
It removes the jump table
It lets opcodes run in parallel
drills.why: The reported gain when CPython adopted it was fifteen to twenty percent, for code that computes the same thing in the same order.

drills.q: Why did CPython 3.14 add an interpreter built from small functions and tail calls?
options: A single function of thousands of lines defeats register allocation, and splitting it fixes that
Tail calls are faster than jumps on modern processors
It allows opcodes to be compiled separately at run time
It was required for free threading
drills.why: The measured gain is three to five percent on the standard benchmark suite. It is a register allocation problem, not a control flow one.

drills.q: What can a JIT know that an ahead of time compiler cannot?
options: Which types, branches and call targets actually occurred in this run
The exact processor model it is running on
The contents of the source file
How much memory is available
drills.why: Knowing the target processor is possible ahead of time too. Knowing that this site has seen two integers ten thousand times running is not.

drills.q: In a specialising interpreter, where does the inline cache live?
options: In the instruction stream, immediately after the instruction it belongs to
In a hash table keyed by instruction address
In the object header of the operands
In a side table written when the function returns
drills.why: Putting it next to the instruction means the interpreter has already loaded the cache line it needs by the time it wants the cache.

drills.q: What are the four steps of specialisation?
options: Observe, assume, guard, and be able to take it back
Parse, compile, link, and load
Count, compile, inline, and unroll
Trace, optimise, verify, and commit
drills.why: The same shape appears in every fast dynamic language runtime under different names. The last step is what makes the second one safe.

drills.q: A specialised instruction's guard fails once. What happens?
options: A counter is decremented and the general operation runs; it stays specialised
It immediately reverts to the general form
The whole function is recompiled
The guard is removed and the specialised path runs anyway
drills.why: One unusual value should not undo a site that is right the rest of the time. The instruction reverts only when the counter has run out.

drills.q: Why is a specialised instruction allowed to assume anything at all?
options: Because the guard in front of it makes a wrong assumption slow rather than incorrect
Because the type system has already proved the assumption
Because the specialisation is only applied to code that cannot change
Because the interpreter re-checks the whole frame at each instruction
drills.why: Deoptimisation is what converts a guess into an optimisation. Without a way back it would be a bug.

options: Compiling costs time and most code runs once, so cheap execution comes first and pays for the compile decision
Different tiers target different processors
The first tier checks types and the second one runs the program
Each tier handles a different language feature
drills.why: The cheap tier also collects the information the expensive tier needs, so the counting is not wasted work.

drills.q: What problem does on stack replacement solve?
options: A function entered once whose loop is already running is hot, and waiting for it to return means waiting forever
Two threads entering the same compiled function at once
Restoring the stack after an exception unwinds through compiled code
Moving a frame from the heap to the stack when it stops escaping
drills.why: It compiles a new version and transfers the running frame into it, moving every live value and the loop counter across mid flight.

drills.q: What does a cached bytecode file do for a program?
options: Skips tokenising and parsing, so the program starts faster and runs the same
Stores an optimised version of the program, so it runs faster
Stores machine code produced by the JIT on a previous run
Records profiling information for the next run to specialise from
drills.why: It holds the same code object the compiler would have produced. Its magic number is rejected outright when the format changed, and a stamp or hash says whether the source is still the same.
